stages.meaning: the time off at the end of the week

history: Week-end is pure English: week plus end. English used it for the end of the week from 1638, and for the free time at the end of the working week from 1879. French writers first used it about English life: a French book of 1906 speaks of the week-end in England. In 1926 the writer Jean Giraudoux uses it about France. The word stayed, with its hyphen and its English shape, and it is masculine: le week-end, ce week-end, bon week-end ! The 1990 spelling reform also accepts weekend, without the hyphen. In Quebec people usually say la fin de semaine, which is the same idea in French words. Remember: in France, a long weekend is un week-end prolongé, or un pont when a public holiday falls nearby.
historyEinfach: Week-end is an English word: week and end. French took it at the start of the 20th century. In French it is masculine: le week-end. Bon week-end! means ‘Have a nice weekend!’. In Quebec, people say la fin de semaine.

elsewhere.text: French took the English word whole. Quebec French translated it instead: la fin de semaine.
